claim: Human groups show a positive manifold across diverse tasks, with a first factor of about 43-44% in the founding studies (40 and 152 groups; 699 people).
agent_test: Run the scaffold and a plain baseline on 5+ diverse task types at equal tokens; check one-factor share and mean inter-task r.

claim: Across a 22-study meta-analysis (1,356 groups) the single factor holds but is weaker: mean inter-task r 0.27, loadings 0.27-0.52, AVE 44% (Riedl) or about 30% (Rowe, squared loadings over 49 loadings). Arithmetic check (inference): loadings of .27-.52 cannot give an AVE of 44%; mean r .27 implies about 27%.
agent_test: Report variance share with both methods when we measure our own cross-task factor.

claim: c predicts out-of-sample criterion tasks, but weakly to moderately and with high heterogeneity: Riedl leave-one-out r=0.40; Rowe pooled r=.26 (95% CI .10-.40, I2=86.5%, 857 groups).
agent_test: Hold out one task family; fit the scaffold's setting on the rest; check transfer.

claim: Member intelligence explains little of c in Woolley (r=0.15 avg, 0.19 max in Study 2; ns in Study 1) but Bates and Gupta found average IQ explains about 80% of group-IQ variance; the g-versus-c contrast is contested.
agent_test: On LLM groups, regress group score on mean member score; Zhou-style design.

claim: Social sensitivity (RME) correlates with c: r=.26 (Woolley S2), .53 face-to-face and .55 online (Engel 2014, 68 groups), min-RME r=.52 (Meslec, 30 groups). Bates and Gupta found only a small added effect (beta .19) once IQ was in the model.
agent_test: Test whether an explicit perspective-taking step (model of other agents' views) lifts multi-agent score beyond base model strength.

claim: Proportion of women predicting c is not robust: significant in Woolley (r=.23) and Engel online (r=.41) and Riedl meta-analysis, but not in any of three Bates and Gupta studies.
agent_test: Not applicable to agent; do not build on gender composition.

claim: Turn-taking equality (low variance in speaking) correlates with c (r=-0.41, Woolley sociometric subset; Engel: communication SD negative), but Bates and Gupta found turn-taking variance unrelated to group IQ. Causal tests are null or indirect: Bates and Gupta Study 3 equal-talk instruction F(2,34)=1.14, p=.33 (40 groups); video vs audio dyads raised turn inequality (26.3 vs 9.1) but CI did not differ (p=.22).
agent_test: Vary speaking-turn balance among LLM agents at equal tokens.

claim: A single c factor is not found in computer-mediated or task-diverse samples in some studies: Graf et al. pooled 745 teams show mean inter-task r=.001 and a bad one-factor fit; Barlow and Dennis 86 virtual groups show no c; Credé and Howardson reanalysis disputes it.
agent_test: Check whether cross-task correlation of our scaffold survives when tasks span types, not just reasoning.

claim: Boundary condition: small samples. Only 6 of 19 samples had power to detect r=.10-.30; coordination structure can create c in virtual groups (thesis r=.339).
agent_test: Use at least 30 tasks and several seeds in any agent test.

claim: LLM populations show a much stronger general factor than humans: 591 LLMs, mean inter-test r 0.73, first factor about 66%, omega hierarchical .94.
agent_test: Compute the first-factor share across our scaffold arms on mixed benchmarks.

claim: LLM groups show a collective general factor: 108 groups, mean inter-task r=0.55, first factor 66.3% (second 18.7%), CFA CFI .967; it is predicted by skill congruence (over 50% RF importance) and mean member g (37%), not group size. Groups were built from only 8 LLMs of 5 provider families (3 Qwen), so independence from shared base ability is untested.
agent_test: Replicate on our agent: vary mix of strong and weak sub-agents, check ACI vs cost.

claim: In LLM groups, more compute and stronger members are not enough: a group with 75% higher cost had 9.7% lower ACI; centralized network with strongest LLM as hub often beat fully connected decentralized one at lower cost.
agent_test: Compare hub-and-spoke vs all-to-all at equal tokens.

claim: Adding agents often hurts: GPT-4.1 groups lose about 8% odds of success per member (OR 0.92); scaling study finds negative returns when single-agent baseline exceeds 45% (beta=-0.236) and error amplification 4.4x to 17.2x. Token-matched (4,800 tokens) in Kim; Tran and Kiela find a single agent best at 500-5k thinking tokens but beaten at 100 tokens.
agent_test: Test single scaffolded agent vs N parallel agents at equal tokens; expect single to win on sequential tasks.

claim: Human-AI combinations on average do worse than the best of human or AI alone on decision tasks (g=-0.27) but not on creation tasks (g=0.19, ns).
agent_test: Compare scaffold with vs without critic step on decision versus generation tasks.

claim: Majority voting beats multi-round debate on most benchmarks at the models tested (Qwen2.5-7B .7691 vs .7377; Llama3.1-8B .7242 vs .6990).
agent_test: Compare vote of N samples vs N-agent debate at equal tokens.

claim: LLM groups fail to pool distributed information: 30.1% multi-agent accuracy vs 80.7% with full information; humans also fall short (0.385 vs 0.604). A two-stage structured exchange (share 1-2 facts plus one doubt, then decide) raised GPT-4.1 from .037 to .800 (18 tasks, 5 runs, 4 agents).
agent_test: Test an explicit shared-facts step on hidden-profile tasks.

claim: A theory-of-mind prompt did NOT raise overall success in a powered test (GPT-4.1, 10 agents, 200 groups per arm); the effect is only a marginal mediation via synergy (ACME .034, p=.053) and emergence share was lower with ToM (18% vs 37% plain). Explicit belief-state text raised ToM inference accuracy in a 3-agent game with three trials (underpowered).
agent_test: A/B a theory-of-mind line on multi-agent tasks at equal tokens with 50+ runs.

claim: Teamwork ability of LLM agents is dominated by one component (71% of variance in eight scores) and tracks general capability (r=0.92 with intelligence index).
agent_test: Check whether teamwork scores are separable from base ability after controlling it.

claim: Task type moderates collaboration gain: scaling relative change ranges +80.8% (decomposable) to -70.0% (sequential).
agent_test: Classify tasks by decomposability before choosing multi-agent.

claim: Dyadic c exists for structured tasks with individual intelligence (beta .33) and confidence (beta .32) as predictors in 105 dyads.
agent_test: Not a priority.

claim: Multi-agent LLM systems fail often (41-86.7% of traces) mostly from design, inter-agent misalignment and weak verification.
agent_test: Add an independent verifier to a multi-agent run and count failure modes.

claim: Instructing human groups to take equal turns did not raise group scores in the one randomised test found (Bates and Gupta Study 3, 40 groups, p=.33), and a video-vs-audio manipulation moved turn inequality without a significant CI difference (99 dyads); the causal role of turn-taking is unproven in humans and untested in LLM groups.
agent_test: If tested in agents: equal-turn forcing vs free order, 50+ runs per arm.

claim: The human first-factor share in pooled data is about 27-30% (mean r .27; Rowe 30.23%), not 44%; Riedl's reported AVE 44% is arithmetically at odds with its loadings of .27-.52 (inference, SI not read).
agent_test: Report variance share with the same method as the comparison set.

claim: Graf's pooled null (r=.001, three factors) uses only five McGrath task types, averages different concrete tasks across studies and mixes face-to-face and computer-mediated samples; task-type collapse and medium are candidate causes, scoring rules untested; the source is a 4-page work-in-progress abstract.
agent_test: Use identical concrete tasks across runs when we test a scaffold factor.

claim: At equal thinking tokens, a single agent usually matches or beats multi-agent designs, with exceptions at very small budgets (100 tokens) and with corrupted context; the 45% single-agent baseline boundary comes from a six-benchmark fit, not a controlled sweep.
agent_test: Run scaffold vs N parallel agents at equal tokens on a task ladder spanning 20-80% single-agent accuracy.

claim: A society of over two million agents showed no measurable collective intelligence on probe tasks (no gain over single frontier models; rarely pooled distributed information).
agent_test: None.

claim: No published test was found of whether a single agent with different scaffolds shows a cross-task general factor; Ilic and Gignac's 66% factor is across 591 models, not scaffolds.
agent_test: Run N scaffolds x 8 task types on one model; compute first-factor share and mean r.

claim: No preregistered large replication of c versus member-IQ exists in the sources found; Bates and Gupta (80 combined groups, latent model: IQ explains about all group-IQ) and Woolley disagree, and Bates and Gupta's group tasks overlap IQ content.
agent_test: None.
